title: Europe's overseas possessions could be a major global asset
gist: Sumantra Maitra argues the simultaneous Ceuta and Falklands crises are causally linked episodes in a US-backed hemispheric turn, and that Europe's 13 overseas territories across six states - currently treated as marginal possessions - are an unexploited strategic and economic asset. His concrete prescriptions: overseas constabulary legions, a pooled overseas territories investment fund for dual-use infrastructure (AI, drones, satellites, ports, undersea cable), and a dedicated intelligence-sharing bloc.

themes.theme: The new American right is not a European ally

insights.claim: The new American right is temperamentally Christian-evangelical and demographically Hispanic, hawkish on the Western Hemisphere, and has convinced itself that Europe is decadent, pacifist and conquered - making Israel and Argentina, not European populists, its chosen allies.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Anyone who assumed a Trump presidency would empower a transatlantic populist bloc mispriced it; the alignment runs through the Western Hemisphere instead.

themes.theme: The underused asset: 13 territories, six states

insights.claim: Six European states possess 13 overseas territories which are by extension territories of the European Union, yet there has been no concerted European effort to develop, resettle, repopulate or strengthen them.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Quantifies the unexploited asset base and identifies exactly where European policy would have to change for it to be monetised or defended.
insights.quote: Currently, six European states possess 13 overseas territories, which are by extension territories of the European Union itself.

insights.claim: Rival powers already run overseas expeditionary networks Europe lacks - Russia's state-directed Africa Corps grown from the rump of Wagner, Turkey's use of military and security companies in Libya, Syria, Somalia and Sudan, and Chinese firms such as Frontier Services Group providing order in exchange for resources.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Private and quasi-state security provision abroad is now standard practice for major powers - a growth market Europe is absent from.
insights.quote: Russia runs a state-directed expeditionary force in Africa, known as the Africa Corps, which originally developed from the rump of the now-defunct Wagner Group.
insights.locator: Other great powers have already recognised

insights.claim: Britain alone lacks the naval and military capacity to permanently defend and redevelop all its worldwide territories, whereas a coordinated CANZUK naval structure would provide a far larger pool of ships, personnel, bases, intelligence and industrial capacity - yet there has been little serious movement toward CANZUK joint commands, banks or investment funds.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: CANZUK institutional formation is the concrete, checkable signal that this thesis is being acted on; its absence to date is the author's main evidence of European drift.
insights.quote: But, despite the economic and military potential, there has been little serious movement towards creating CANZUK joint commands, banks or investment funds.
insights.locator: The second problem is one of scale

insights.claim: The European Union is by design fractured and unsuited to a world of renewed great-power predation, evidenced by Europe blaming Madrid for the Ceuta crisis and half the continent appeasing the United States over Greenland.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Collective EU response is not a reliable hedge for territorial risk; national and minilateral capability is what will actually be deployed.
insights.quote: But the European Union is by design fractured and unsuited for a world of renewed great-power predation.
insights.locator: The response of European states

insights.claim: Imperial politics requires mass and scale, which makes it inherently cosmopolitan and therefore incompatible with the increasingly narrow, inward-looking nationalism now dominant in Europe's major powers.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: A structural reason to doubt that nationalist European governments will build overseas capability, however strategically rational it would be.
insights.quote: Imperial politics requires mass and scale, which automatically makes it overtly cosmopolitan.
insights.locator: The final related problem is political

insights.claim: Populist politics prioritises what is geographically close and immediately visible to voters, making territories thousands of miles away expensive and politically unimportant to defend - a majoritarian short-sightedness the author calls strategically self-defeating.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Predicts under-defence of distant territories by European populist governments, which is precisely the condition rivals are probing.
insights.quote: Justifying overseas territories thousands of miles away becomes expensive and politically unimportant.
insights.locator: Populist politics also tends to prioritise issues

insights.claim: European major powers want to be seen as quasi-imperial entities with faraway territories while refusing the imperial policies that would sustain them - the author's summary being that the ideas of a British Empire and Little England cannot coexist.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Names the internal contradiction that will determine whether Britain actually contests the Falklands challenge or concedes it.
insights.quote: The ideas of a British Empire and Little England cannot coexist.
insights.locator: The paradox for European major powers

insights.claim: A data centre in a British overseas territory in the Pacific would create demand for housing, schools, transport, telecommunications and energy infrastructure, seeding new communities around an existing possession - with parallel projects in AI research, drone manufacturing, satellite communications, renewable energy, ports and advanced manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: An explicit strategic case for siting AI and data infrastructure in remote sovereign territories - a policy-driven demand channel for dual-use compute buildout.
insights.quote: A data centre in a British overseas territory in the Pacific, for example, could create demand for housing, schools, cafes, restaurants, transport, telecommunications, energy infrastructure and other services.
insights.locator: That brand of majoritarian populism is strategically short-sighted

insights.claim: European powers should create permanent overseas guards and legions - small professional constabulary units recruited from their own territories and partner states, building on existing military exchanges with countries such as Fiji and Nepal, and a systematic French Foreign Legion recruitment pipeline from Francophone countries.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Small, specialised constabulary forces are the low-cost way to make distant territories defensible - watch for recruitment-pipeline announcements as the leading signal.
insights.quote: First, they should create permanent overseas guards and legions: small, highly professional constabulary units recruited from their own territories, and from willing partner states with established military traditions.

insights.claim: European states with overseas territories should pool resources into an overseas territories investment fund or sovereign defence-related bank dedicated to infrastructure and dual-use technology, prioritising AI, drones, satellite communications, ports, renewable energy, undersea infrastructure, cybersecurity and advanced manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: A named sector list for where state capital would flow if this agenda is adopted - dual-use infrastructure in remote maritime territories.

insights.claim: The proposed network has a direct historical precedent in the 19th-century telegraph and steamship systems that connected European territories and commercial interests, with digital communications, satellites, autonomous systems and energy infrastructure playing the modern equivalent role.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Frames undersea cable and satellite networks as the strategic chokepoint infrastructure of the coming period, as telegraph was in the 19th century.
insights.quote: The concept would have a historical precedent in the telegraph and steamship networks that connected European territories and commercial interests across the world during the 19th century.

insights.claim: It was fear of conquest and dismemberment under great-power competition - not commercial appetite alone - that drove European expansion from the 16th century, and Europe today lacks not money or talent but the strategic spark to restart that competitive dynamic.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: If competitive fear is the actual trigger, escalating pressure on Ceuta and the Falklands may itself catalyse the European rearmament this piece advocates.
insights.quote: European major powers today do not lack money, talent or interest. What they lack is a strategic spark capable of restarting that competitive dynamic.
insights.locator: More than any other causal mechanism

insights.claim: A multipolar world is characteristically imperial and unlikely to favour narrow nationalism, because multipolarity by definition creates strategic conditions that small states cannot manage alone - so 19th-century problems require 19th-century templates.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: The core prediction: scale blocs, not nation states, will be the viable units - a lens for judging which European security groupings gain traction.
insights.quote: Ceuta and the Falklands should therefore remind Spain, Britain and the rest of Europe’s major players, that 19th-century problems will require 19th-century templates.
insights.locator: A multipolar world is characteristically imperial
